hypothesis.title: Adaptive Proximity Regularization for Inference-Time Alignment via Coverage-Aware Reward Hacking Mitigation
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes an adaptive proximity regularization method for inference-time alignment that dynamically adjusts the strength of regularization based on the coverage of high-quality responses in the pre-trained policy. By analyzing the coverage properties of the policy, the method identifies regions where reward hacking is more likely and applies stronger regularization there. The approach combines coverage estimation with a modified MBR objective to balance reward optimization and proximity to the reference policy. Evaluation uses Best-of-N baselines with varying N on tasks from AlpacaFarm and Anthropic's hh-rlhf datasets, measuring both reward model scores and human preference metrics to demonstrate improved robustness against reward hacking.
hypothesis.gap: Existing inference-time alignment methods like MBR-BoN and InferenceTimePessimism apply fixed regularization or pessimism without considering the varying coverage of high-quality responses across different prompts. This leaves open the question of how to adaptively adjust alignment strategies based on coverage properties.
hypothesis.approach: The proposed method estimates coverage of high-quality responses via reward model thresholds and dynamically adjusts MBR regularization strength. For prompts with low coverage (indicating sparse high-quality regions), stronger regularization is applied to prevent reward hacking. For high-coverage prompts, weaker regularization allows more aggressive reward optimization.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compared against Best-of-N, MBR-BoN, and InferenceTimePessimism baselines on AlpacaFarm and hh-rlhf datasets. Metrics include reward model scores, human preference ratings, and reward hacking detection rates. Ablation studies vary coverage estimation methods and regularization schedules.

refined.title: Adaptive Proximity Regularization for Inference-Time Alignment via Coverage-Aware Reward Hacking Mitigation
refined.summary: This paper proposes an adaptive proximity regularization method for inference-time alignment that dynamically adjusts the strength of regularization based on the coverage of high-quality responses in the pre-trained policy. By analyzing the coverage properties of the policy, the method identifies regions where reward hacking is more likely and applies stronger regularization there. The approach combines coverage estimation with a modified MBR objective to balance reward optimization and proximity to the reference policy. Evaluation uses Best-of-N baselines with varying N on tasks from AlpacaFarm and Anthropic's hh-rlhf datasets, measuring both reward model scores and human preference metrics to demonstrate improved robustness against reward hacking.
refined.gap: Existing inference-time alignment methods like MBR-BoN apply fixed regularization strength without considering the varying coverage of high-quality responses across prompts. While ref-004's InferenceTimePessimism rejects low-reward samples adaptively, it does not explicitly model coverage to adjust regularization strength. This leaves open the question of how to dynamically balance reward optimization and proximity based on coverage.
refined.approach: The method estimates coverage as the fraction of samples exceeding a reward threshold (set at the 75th percentile of the reward distribution for the prompt). For low-coverage prompts (≤25%), MBR regularization weight α is set to 1.0; for high-coverage prompts (>25%), α is 0.5. The modified MBR objective is: argmax_y [E_{y'∼p(y|x)}[r(y',x)] + α·log p(y|x)], where r is the reward model, p(y|x) is the reference policy, and α is coverage-dependent. This differs from ref-003's fixed α=1.0 by introducing coverage-aware adaptation.
refined.evaluation: Compared against Best-of-N (ref-003), MBR-BoN (ref-003), and InferenceTimePessimism (ref-004) on AlpacaFarm and hh-rlhf datasets. Metrics: (1) reward model score, (2) human preference ratings (from ref-003), (3) reward hacking rate measured as the fraction of responses with reward > threshold but human preference < 0.5. Ablation studies test fixed α=1.0 vs. coverage-aware α, and threshold settings (50th vs. 75th percentile).

hypothesis.title: Inference-Time Pessimism with MBR Regularization for Scalable Safe Alignment
hypothesis.summary: We propose integrating InferenceTimePessimism with Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) regularization to improve safety alignment during inference. The method combines pessimistic rejection sampling with MBR's proximity regularization to mitigate reward hacking while ensuring safe response generation. It is validated on safety benchmarks like HarmBench and StrongREJECT, comparing against BoN and LARA baselines using AU-PRC and attack success rate metrics.
hypothesis.gap: Existing inference-time alignment methods like BoN and LARA either degrade with increased compute or lack formal safety guarantees under imperfect reward models.
hypothesis.approach: Adapt InferenceTimePessimism's rejection sampling framework to incorporate MBR's proximity regularization. During decoding, candidate responses are scored using both a reward model and an MBR-derived proximity term, with pessimistic thresholds dynamically adjusted based on reward uncertainty.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare against BoN, LARA, and vanilla MBR decoding on HarmBench and StrongREJECT. Use AU-PRC for safety classification and attack success rate for jailbreaking robustness. Include ablations on MBR weight and pessimism thresholds.

refined.title: Inference-Time Pessimism with MBR Regularization for Scalable Safe Alignment
refined.summary: We propose integrating InferenceTimePessimism's rejection sampling with MBR regularization to mitigate reward hacking while ensuring safe response generation under imperfect reward models. The method combines pessimistic thresholds calibrated via reward uncertainty with MBR's proximity regularization to reference policies. It is evaluated on HarmBench and StrongREJECT against BoN, LARA, and MBR-BoN baselines using AU-PRC and attack success rate metrics, with ablations isolating the contributions of pessimism and MBR regularization.
refined.gap: Ref-004 shows InferenceTimePessimism avoids reward hacking degradation with increased compute but does not explicitly regularize response proximity to reference policies. Ref-003 demonstrates MBR regularization mitigates reward hacking but lacks formal safety guarantees under scaling. No work combines both to ensure scalable, safe alignment with provable properties.
refined.approach: Implement a two-phase inference-time framework: (1) Rejection sampling with pessimistic thresholds (ref-004) that lower-bound reward estimates by reward model uncertainty, and (2) MBR regularization (ref-003) that scores candidates by expected loss to a reference policy. The final response is the highest-scoring candidate passing the pessimistic threshold. The method differs from ref-004 by adding MBR as a secondary filter and from ref-003 by incorporating pessimism to handle reward uncertainty.
refined.evaluation: Compare against BoN (ref-004), LARA (ref-012), and MBR-BoN (ref-003) on HarmBench (ref-014) and StrongREJECT (ref-021) using AU-PRC for safety classification and attack success rate for jailbreaking robustness. Use the same reward model and reference policy for all methods. Ablations include: (1) pessimism-only (no MBR), (2) MBR-only (no pessimism), and (3) varying MBR weight to isolate regularization impact.

hypothesis.title: Adaptive Reward Model Pessimism for Scaling-Monotonic Inference-Time Alignment
hypothesis.summary: We propose a method to improve inference-time alignment by adaptively applying pessimism to reward model scores during Best-of-N sampling, ensuring performance does not degrade with increased N. The approach uses a dynamic penalty term based on reward model uncertainty, estimated via bootstrapped reward model ensembles. We validate this by comparing against fixed-penalty baselines and standard Best-of-N on tasks with varying prompt difficulty, measuring both reward model score and human evaluation metrics.
hypothesis.gap: Existing methods like Best-of-N suffer from reward hacking when N is large, and while InferenceTimePessimism mitigates this, it does not adaptively adjust pessimism based on reward model confidence, leading to suboptimal performance on easy prompts.
hypothesis.approach: Introduce a dynamic pessimism penalty that scales with reward model uncertainty, estimated via bootstrapped ensembles. For each generated response, the reward score is adjusted by a term proportional to the standard deviation of bootstrapped reward estimates. This adjusted score is used for ranking in Best-of-N sampling.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare against standard Best-of-N, fixed-penalty Best-of-N, and InferenceTimePessimism on datasets with varying prompt difficulties (e.g., HH-RLHF, AlpacaFarm). Measure reward model score, human evaluation of response quality, and compute the percentage of cases where performance improves with increased N (scaling monotonicity).

However, ref-004 states that InferenceTimePessimism 'implements the principle of pessimism in the face of uncertainty via rejection sampling' and 'its performance is optimal and does not degrade with N,' which contradicts the claim that it fails to adapt to confidence or underperforms on easy prompts. Additionally, the hypothesis asserts that 'existing methods like Best-of-N suffer from reward hacking when N is large,' but ref-002 shows that 'compute-optimal' strategies can outperform larger models without degradation, suggesting some Best-of-N variants avoid this issue.

refined.title: Adaptive Reward Model Pessimism for Scaling-Monotonic Inference-Time Alignment
refined.summary: We propose a method to improve inference-time alignment by adaptively applying pessimism to reward model scores during Best-of-N sampling, ensuring performance does not degrade with increased N. The approach uses a dynamic penalty term proportional to the standard deviation of bootstrapped reward model ensembles. We validate this by comparing against standard Best-of-N, fixed-penalty baselines, and InferenceTimePessimism on datasets with varying prompt difficulties, measuring both reward model score and human evaluation metrics.
refined.gap: Existing pessimism methods (ref-004) apply uniform penalties regardless of reward model confidence, failing to exploit varying uncertainty across prompts. While InferenceTimePessimism prevents reward hacking, it does not adapt penalties to reward model uncertainty, leading to suboptimal performance on easy prompts where over-pessimism is unnecessary. Best-of-N (ref-002) suffers from reward hacking when N is large.
refined.approach: Introduce a dynamic pessimism penalty δ = k·σ, where σ is the standard deviation of bootstrapped reward estimates from an ensemble of 10 models trained on resampled preference data, and k ≥ 1 is a constant. For each generated response, the reward score R is adjusted to R' = R − δ. This adjusted score is used for ranking in Best-of-N sampling. The core mechanism differs from ref-004 by replacing fixed rejection thresholds with adaptive penalties tied to estimated uncertainty.
refined.evaluation: Compare against standard Best-of-N, fixed-penalty Best-of-N (δ = 0.1), and InferenceTimePessimism (ref-004) on HH-RLHF and AlpacaFarm datasets. Stratify prompts by difficulty using reward model score quartiles (Q1: hard, Q4: easy). Measure reward model score, human evaluation of response quality, and scaling monotonicity as the percentage of prompts where performance improves with N = 100 vs. N = 10. Include an ablation with ground-truth uncertainty (synthetic data) to isolate the penalty mechanism's effect.

hypothesis.title: Adaptive Compute-Optimal Inference-Time Alignment with Coverage-Aware Pessimism
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes an adaptive inference-time alignment method that combines compute-optimal scaling with coverage-aware pessimism to mitigate reward hacking. The approach dynamically allocates test-time compute based on prompt difficulty while incorporating pessimism to reject low-quality responses. It is validated on diverse tasks using reward model benchmarks, comparing performance against fixed compute baselines and measuring scaling efficiency through FLOPs-matched evaluations.
hypothesis.gap: Existing methods like Best-of-N and InferenceTimePessimism either fail to adapt compute allocation to prompt difficulty or lack formal coverage guarantees, leading to suboptimal performance or reward hacking under imperfect reward models.
hypothesis.approach: The method integrates a compute-optimal allocation strategy with pessimism-based rejection sampling. It estimates prompt difficulty via reward model uncertainty, allocates compute proportionally, and applies pessimism to reject responses below a calibrated threshold. The algorithm adaptively balances exploration (via compute scaling) and exploitation (via pessimism).
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include Best-of-N, InferenceTimePessimism, and fixed compute methods. Metrics are response quality (reward model scores), reward hacking rates, and compute efficiency (performance per FLOP). Experiments use synthetic and real-world datasets with varying reward model accuracies.

However, ref-004 explicitly states that InferenceTimePessimism 'mitigates reward hacking through deliberate use of inference-time compute' and 'is scaling-monotonic' (does not degrade with N), contradicting the claim about lacking formal coverage guarantees. Additionally, ref-002 demonstrates compute-optimal allocation strategies that adapt compute to prompt difficulty, contradicting the claim that Best-of-N fails to adapt compute allocation.

refined.title: Adaptive Compute-Optimal Inference-Time Alignment with Coverage-Aware Pessimism
refined.summary: This paper proposes an adaptive inference-time alignment method that combines compute-optimal allocation with pessimism-based rejection sampling. The approach estimates prompt difficulty via reward model uncertainty, allocates compute proportionally, and rejects responses below a calibrated threshold. It is evaluated on synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing against Best-of-N, InferenceTimePessimism, and fixed compute baselines, with metrics including response quality, reward hacking rates, and compute efficiency.
refined.gap: While ref-002 shows compute-optimal strategies adapt compute to prompt difficulty and ref-004 proves InferenceTimePessimism has formal coverage guarantees, no method combines both to balance adaptive compute allocation with pessimism under imperfect reward models. Existing work either optimizes compute allocation (ref-002) or applies pessimism (ref-004), but does not integrate both to mitigate reward hacking while maintaining scaling efficiency.
refined.approach: The method uses a two-stage process: (1) Estimate prompt difficulty via reward model uncertainty (standard deviation of reward scores over N samples), allocating compute as N = k * (1 + σ/μ), where σ is uncertainty, μ is mean reward, and k is a base sample count. (2) Apply pessimism by rejecting responses with scores below a threshold τ, where τ = μ - c * σ, with c a constant. The algorithm adaptively balances compute allocation (ref-002) and pessimism (ref-004) to prevent over-optimization. The core difference from ref-002 (fixed k) and ref-004 (fixed N) is the dynamic N and τ based on reward model uncertainty.
refined.evaluation: Baselines: Best-of-N (ref-002), InferenceTimePessimism (ref-004), and fixed compute (N=100). Datasets: Synthetic (ref-006) and real-world (ref-003, ref-004). Metrics: (1) Response quality (proxy reward score), (2) Reward hacking rate (difference between proxy and gold reward scores, ref-006), (3) Compute efficiency (performance per FLOP, ref-002). Ablations: (1) Fixed vs. adaptive N, (2) Pessimism threshold τ vs. no rejection, (3) Uncertainty estimation method (σ vs. fixed σ=0). The evaluation tests whether adaptive N and τ reduce reward hacking while maintaining compute efficiency compared to baselines.

hypothesis.title: Compute-Optimal Safety Reasoning via Adaptive Prompt Difficulty Estimation
hypothesis.summary: This paper introduces a compute-optimal framework for safety reasoning that adapts the amount of inference-time computation based on the estimated difficulty of detecting harmful content in a prompt. By training a lightweight classifier to predict prompt difficulty from features like perplexity and syntactic complexity, the method allocates more Best-of-N sampling iterations to ambiguous cases while using minimal computation for clearly safe/unsafe prompts. The approach is validated on HarmBench and StrongREJECT datasets, showing improved safety-efficiency tradeoffs compared to fixed-compute baselines.
hypothesis.gap: Current safety reasoning methods like Constitutional AI and ShieldGemma apply fixed computational budgets regardless of prompt difficulty, overlooking the potential efficiency gains from adaptive computation allocation.
hypothesis.approach: A two-stage process: (1) Train a difficulty estimator using prompt features and labeled safety annotations; (2) Use the estimator at inference time to dynamically set N for Best-of-N sampling. The estimator is trained on features including token perplexity, syntactic complexity scores, and embedding distances to safety guidelines.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compared against fixed-N Best-of-N baselines on HarmBench and StrongREJECT. Metrics include attack success rates (ASR), false positive rates (FPR), and compute efficiency (queries/sec). Ablation studies vary difficulty estimation features and estimator architectures.

However, ref-007 does not mention Constitutional AI or ShieldGemma, and its focus is on safety reasoning via guidelines rather than fixed computational budgets. The gap claim is unsupported by the cited references, as none explicitly state or imply that prior methods overlook adaptive computation allocation.

Additionally, the ablation studies are not described in terms of how they isolate the effect of difficulty estimation features versus other components. The exact metrics for 'syntactic complexity scores' and 'embedding distances to safety guidelines' are also undefined, making replication difficult.

This would better isolate the contribution of the difficulty estimation mechanism.

refined.summary: This work introduces a method to mitigate reward hacking in Best-of-N sampling by dynamically adjusting the strength of Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) regularization based on reward model uncertainty. refined.approach: We extend MBR-BoN by introducing a learnable temperature parameter that modulates the proximity term based on reward model confidence. The temperature is optimized via meta-learning on a held-out validation set, allowing the system to adjust regularization strength per prompt. The objective function is: argmax_{y} [λ(r(y) - r_0) + (1 - λ) log p(y|x)], where λ = σ(τ * (c - c_0)), τ is the temperature parameter, c is reward model confidence, c_0 is a threshold, and σ is the sigmoid function. refined.evaluation: Baselines include vanilla Best-of-N (ref-002), MBR-BoN (ref-003), and DPO (ref-010). Ablation studies isolate the dynamic temperature mechanism by comparing against a fixed-weight variant.

hypothesis.title: Lagrangian Reward Augmentation for Safety-Constrained Best-of-N Sampling
hypothesis.summary: This paper extends Lagrangian Reward Augmentation (LARA) to safety-constrained Best-of-N sampling, enabling explicit safety cost constraints during inference. The method calibrates a dual variable to balance reward and safety costs, ensuring compliance without manual penalty tuning. It is validated on safety benchmarks, comparing helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoffs against unconstrained BoN and RLHF baselines.
hypothesis.gap: Existing inference-time alignment methods like BoN lack formal safety guarantees and require manual penalty tuning, risking either excessive harm or overly conservative responses.
hypothesis.approach: LARA dualizes the safety constraint, reducing the problem to a one-dimensional optimization over a dual variable. The variable is calibrated on a small set of safety-critical prompts, defining an augmented reward for BoN reranking. The method guarantees constraint satisfaction in expectation when the dual variable is correctly calibrated.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include vanilla BoN, MBR-BoN, and RLHF. Metrics are helpfulness (reward model scores), harmlessness (safety model scores), and constraint violation rates. Experiments use HarmBench and Anthropic's safety datasets, with ablation studies on calibration set size.

The augmented reward is used for BoN reranking, ensuring constraint satisfaction in expectation. It is evaluated on HarmBench and Anthropic's safety datasets, comparing helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoffs against unconstrained BoN, MBR-BoN, and RLHF baselines.

refined.approach: LARA dualizes the safety constraint, reducing the problem to a one-dimensional convex optimization over a nonnegative dual variable. The variable is calibrated on a small set of safety-critical prompts (e.g., 100 from HarmBench) to define an augmented reward: R_aug = R - λC, where R is the reward model score, C is the cost model score, and λ is the dual variable. The augmented reward is used for BoN reranking. The method guarantees constraint satisfaction in expectation when λ is correctly calibrated, differing from ref-012's general LARA by explicitly isolating the dual-variable calibration step.

Experiments use HarmBench (ref-014) and Anthropic's safety datasets (ref-004). Ablation studies compare LARA-BoN with a version where λ is replaced by a manually tuned penalty coefficient, and test calibration set sizes (10, 50, 100 prompts). The safety-critical calibration set is defined as prompts with the highest cost model scores in the training data.
